h1: Chilli in beer: picking the pepper and controlling the heat
title: Chilli in Beer: Picking the Pepper | Craft Beer School
desc: How brewers choose chillies for beer, extract heat and flavour safely and dose capsaicin with bench trials so every batch has the same kick.
teaser: Kashmiri for colour, Guntur for heat, bhut jolokia for regret. How to pick the pepper and dose it so the beer stays drinkable.
standfirst: Chilli beer goes wrong in two ways: no heat at all or so much that nobody orders a second. Picking the right pepper and dosing it by measurement, not by handful, keeps you between those two.
sections: Heat and flavour are separate decisions

A chilli brings two things to beer. The first is heat, from capsaicin and its relatives. The second is flavour and aroma: fruity, grassy, smoky or earthy notes from the flesh and skin. Good chilli beers choose both on purpose.

Capsaicin is concentrated in the pale pith that holds the seeds, not in the seeds themselves. Removing the pith and seeds cuts heat sharply while keeping most of the flavour. That gives you a lever before you even think about dose.

India gives brewers an unusually wide choice.

  • Kashmiri. Mild, with strong red colour and a sweet, paprika-like flavour. Useful when you want chilli character and a warm glow without real burn.
  • Byadgi. Similar role, deep colour, low heat, slightly smoky. A good partner for amber ales and red lagers.
  • Guntur. Properly hot with a sharp, clean heat. Use a little for a noticeable kick.
  • Bhut jolokia. Among the hottest chillies in the world. A tiny amount goes a very long way, with a fruity flavour behind it.
  • Fresh green chillies and jalapeños. Grassy, vegetal and bright. Good in a pale lager or a light wheat beer.
  • Smoked chillies such as chipotle. Smoke and dried fruit, at home in porters and stouts.

Think about the base beer too. A crisp lager shows every chilli note. A rich stout hides heat and flavour, so it needs more. Our guide to brewing with Indian spices covers the wider spice cupboard.
Getting the heat into the beer

Capsaicin dissolves much better in alcohol and fat than in water, which shapes the method.

The most controllable approach is a tincture. Soak chopped or crushed dried chillies in a neutral spirit such as vodka for a few days, then strain. The spirit extracts heat efficiently and keeps the chillies clean. You end up with a concentrate you can measure in millilitres.

The other route is a direct addition to the fermenter or conditioning tank, after fermentation has finished. Toast dried chillies lightly in a dry pan to lift the flavour and reduce raw grassiness, then add them in a sanitised mesh bag. Fresh chillies carry wild microbes on the skin, so blanch them briefly or soak them in spirit first.

Avoid putting chillies in the boil unless you want a harsh, vegetal heat that you cannot easily control. Boil additions are hard to repeat batch to batch.

Never dose a full tank by feel. Pull finished beer and run a bench trial. Measure 100 ml portions into glasses and add the tincture with a 1 ml graduated pipette: 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5 ml, for example. Taste blind with two or three people and choose the level you want.

Then scale it. If 0.2 ml in 100 ml is right, a 500 litre tank needs 1 litre of tincture. Because the tincture is a fixed recipe, the next batch can be dosed the same way and checked again.

With direct additions, taste the tank every day. Heat extraction keeps going and can climb fast. Pull the bag as soon as the beer reaches about 80% of the heat you want, because carbonation makes the burn feel stronger in the glass.

Heat builds with every sip. A beer that tastes pleasantly warm on the first mouthful can feel aggressive by the bottom of a pint. Aim lower than you think on the first release and listen to customers.

Carbonation, alcohol and bitterness all make capsaicin feel hotter. Keep bitterness modest, perhaps 15 to 25 IBU in a chilli lager. Consider serving a slightly smaller pour. Our guide to beer and spicy food heat explains the interaction in more detail.

Label the heat clearly on the menu. Somebody ordering a chilli beer with a biryani needs to know what they are getting.

Record the chilli variety, supplier, whether you removed pith and seeds, toasting time, tincture ratio and final dose per litre. Chilli heat varies between harvests and suppliers, so rerun the bench trial each time you buy a new lot.

Treating a flavour addition as a measured, repeatable process is part of moving from homebrew habits to professional practice. The same logic applies to fruit, spice and coffee.
faqs: When should I add chilli to beer?
After fermentation has finished, either as a tincture made in neutral spirit or as toasted chillies in a sanitised bag. Boil additions are harsh and hard to repeat.
How do I make a chilli beer less hot?
Blend with unspiced beer from the same batch. Next time remove the pith and seeds, use a milder variety or dose less after a bench trial.
Which Indian chilli is best for beer?
It depends on the goal. Kashmiri and byadgi give colour and gentle warmth, Guntur gives clean heat and bhut jolokia gives extreme heat in tiny amounts.
